title: Sitting With a Problem You Can't Solve Yet
summary: When the dashboard goes red, the urge is to do something now. How to stop the bleeding fast, keep the cause question open, and avoid the first idea that sticks.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The alert fires at 4:40 on a Friday, because of course it does. Checkout errors are climbing, the dashboard is going red, and the incident channel fills up faster than anyone can read it. Two minutes in, someone types "roll back the last deploy?" and three people react with a thumbs up.

Rolling back might be exactly right. The moment worth slowing down for comes later, when the graph turns green and everyone wants to call it fixed. Green means the bleeding stopped. It says nothing about why it started.

This post is about that gap: staying with a problem you don't understand yet, long enough to actually understand it, without becoming the person who blocks every decision.

Two ways to react to a mess

In 1977, Harvard Business School professor Abraham Zaleznik wrote an essay that still gets assigned in management courses, Managers and Leaders: Are They Different? HBR's summary of it draws the line around chaos and order. Managers "instinctively try to resolve problems quickly, sometimes before they fully understand a problem's significance." Leaders "tolerate chaos and lack of structure and are willing to delay closure in order to understand the issues more fully" (full reprint).

Zaleznik placed that difference deep in a person's psyche. I'm less sure it's a personality type. On engineering teams it looks more like a habit, and habits can be practiced. Plenty of people who look unshakable during an outage just have more reps.

The split isn't good versus bad either. You want the fast, order-restoring reflex on the rollback. You want the person who can leave a question open on the postmortem. Trouble starts when the first reflex does both jobs, and "the graph is green" slides into "we know what happened."

Why we close too early

Doing something is visible. A rollback shows up in the channel, a closed ticket shows up in standup, a hotfix has a PR number. "Still investigating" sounds like you're stuck, even when it's the most honest status you have.

There's also the plain discomfort of not knowing. An open incident sits in the back of your head all evening. Closing it, even on a guess, makes that feeling stop, so a guess that ends the meeting starts to look a lot like an answer.

Under pressure, with your manager in the channel, the visible move wins almost every time. That's exactly why it helps to decide beforehand what "done" means, before the adrenaline gets a vote.

What an early fix costs

A fast fix often treats the symptom. Say the service runs out of database connections every few days. Restarting it works every time, so it becomes the runbook. Six weeks later someone finally finds the code path that never returns a connection to the pool, and realizes the restarts were covering for it the whole time.

The second cost is sneakier: the first idea tends to stick. Psychologists call this the Einstellung effect. In a 2008 study, Merim Bilalić, Peter McLeod and Fernand Gobet tracked the eye movements of expert chess players who had already spotted a familiar solution. The players said they were looking for a better move. Their eyes kept going back to the squares tied to the solution they already had (Why good thoughts block better ones). The authors suggest the same mechanism may sit behind confirmation bias more broadly.

That was chess, not production. Still, anyone who has debugged under pressure will recognize it. Google's SRE book lists the same trap among common troubleshooting mistakes: "latching on to causes of past problems, reasoning that since it happened once, it must be happening again." It also warns against chasing correlations that turn out to be coincidence (Effective Troubleshooting). The deploy at 4:30 and the errors at 4:40 line up nicely. That could be the cause, or two things that happened on the same Friday.

Stop the bleeding, keep the question open

None of this means you should wait before acting. The SRE book is blunt about it: "Your first response in a major outage may be to start troubleshooting and try to find a root cause as quickly as possible. Ignore that instinct!" Make the system work as well as it can first, then investigate.

So run two clocks. The mitigation clock counts in minutes: roll back, fail over, shed load, whatever restores service. The understanding clock counts in hours or days, and it keeps running after the graph turns green. Holding the answer open happens on the second clock only.

This also separates patience from dithering, which can look alike from across the room. Dithering avoids the problem because deciding feels scary. Holding the question open keeps working on it: you name a hypothesis, decide what evidence would rule it out, and go check. The SRE book describes troubleshooting the same way, as repeatedly proposing causes and testing them.

Four lines for the incident channel

Known: checkout 5xx went from 0.2% to 6% at 16:38, only on the EU cluster. Suspect: the 16:30 deploy, not confirmed. Don't know yet: why only EU. Next check: compare EU and US config diffs, back in 15 minutes.

A note like that lets the team act fast on the first line and stay honest about the third.

Practice it on small problems

Incidents are a terrible place to learn this for the first time. Small daily problems work much better:

  • Notice the urge. When you catch yourself reaching for a fix before you can explain the bug, say it to yourself. Naming it is often enough to buy one more look.
  • Write the one-sentence cause. After mitigation, try to write why it broke in one plain sentence. If you can't, the ticket stays open, labeled "mitigated."
  • List two other explanations. Before you commit to the first theory, write down two more and what would tell them apart. It's a cheap counter to the Einstellung effect.
  • Timebox the open question. "We investigate until Tuesday, then decide with what we have" keeps patience from sliding into avoidance.
  • Close the loop in a postmortem. A blameless review is where the understanding clock finally stops.

Meetings deserve the same treatment. Some rooms want everyone to leave with a decision, even when nobody understands the problem well enough to make one. "Let's leave today with a clear list of what we know and what we don't, and decide on Thursday" is an unpopular sentence. It's also often the most useful thing said all afternoon.

Try this week

  • Next time something breaks, post the four lines (known, suspect, don't know yet, next check) before or right after you mitigate.
  • Find one ticket closed after a restart or a retry, and write its cause in one sentence. If you can't, reopen it as "mitigated."
  • For the bug you're on now, write down two explanations besides your favorite one.

faqs.q: Should I investigate the root cause before rolling back during an incident?
faqs.a: No. Restore service first. Google's SRE book says your first instinct in a major outage may be to hunt for the root cause, and tells you to ignore it and make the system work as well as it can. Roll back or mitigate quickly, then keep investigating after the graph turns green.

faqs.q: What does tolerance for ambiguity mean for an engineer?
faqs.a: It means you can leave a problem open, without a confirmed cause, long enough to understand it, instead of closing it on the first plausible guess. In practice: say what you know, what you only suspect and what you don't know yet, and keep testing hypotheses until one holds.

It's when a familiar first idea blocks you from finding a better one. In a 2008 eye-tracking study, expert chess players who had found a familiar solution said they were searching for a better move, but their eyes kept returning to squares linked to the solution they already had.

faqs.q: How is keeping a problem open different from being indecisive?
faqs.a: Indecision avoids the problem. Keeping it open means you keep working on it: you name a hypothesis, decide what evidence would rule it out and go check. Put a timebox on it, so the team decides on a known date with the best information it has.

faqs.q: How do I practice this outside of incidents?
faqs.a: Use small daily bugs. Before fixing one, try to explain its cause in one sentence. Write down two explanations besides your first one. Keep tickets that were only restarted or retried open as mitigated until someone can explain the cause.
